name: Clavio
tagline: A small paid single-purpose app sold direct from its own site; the exact feature set is not independently verified here.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This is a small independent app sold straight from its own domain, which is almost always the profile of a focused utility rather than a platform with a data or network moat. Apps in that shape clone surprisingly well: the core loop is usually one screen, one local store, and a handful of keyboard shortcuts. What does not clone in one session is the finish, the native feel, the settings nobody notices until they are missing, and whatever sync or mobile side exists. We have low confidence on the specifics here, so treat this as a shape judgement, not a feature-by-feature teardown. Read the product page first, then decide whether the part you actually use is the easy 80 percent or the annoying 20 percent.
coreLoopDIY: You get a local, single-user version of the app's main screen and its core action, persisted to a file on your own machine.
requirements: A coding agent with web access, so it can read the product page before it builds
Somewhere to run it locally, or a free host if you want it on more than one machine
whatYouLose: Native polish: real keyboard handling, window behaviour, animations that do not feel like a school project
Cross-device sync, if the paid version has it, since your clone stores everything in one local file
Mobile, which is a separate build and not part of any one-shot
Updates, bug fixes, and someone to email when it breaks
Whatever integrations exist with tools you already use, each one being its own OAuth adventure
moatNotes: Indie utilities defend themselves with taste and small details, not lock-in. That is a real moat, just not a technical one.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a focused app that already works costs less than a weekend of your time, and the paid version has already lost the arguments you are about to have with yourself about layout, shortcuts, and edge cases. People buying direct from a small site are usually buying the author's judgement, not a feature list. A clone gets you the mechanics and none of the decisions.
notes: Low-information entry: the verdict here is about the shape of the product, not a line-by-line comparison.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal clone of the app at https://clavioapp.com/.

Step 1, research before code:
- Fetch and read https://clavioapp.com/ including any pricing, features, docs, or changelog pages you can reach.
- Write SPEC.md listing the three core user actions the product exists to do, plus anything you saw that is clearly out of scope for a personal build (accounts, billing, teams, mobile apps, integrations).
- If the site is unreachable, stop and tell me instead of guessing at features.

Step 2, stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind.
- better-sqlite3 for storage, a single data.db file in the project root.
- No auth, no accounts, no analytics, no telemetry, no cloud services. Single user on localhost.
- Any API keys go in .env.local, read via process.env, and .env.local goes in .gitignore. Commit .env.example instead.

Step 3, build only the core loop from SPEC.md:
- One primary screen that does the main thing, with real keyboard shortcuts for the two most common actions.
- Full create, edit, delete, and list of whatever the core object is, with a fast text filter.
- JSON export and JSON import of everything, so the data is never trapped.
- Seed the database with five realistic example records on first run.

Out of scope, do not build: sign-up flows, payments, multi-user anything, email, notifications, third-party integrations, a mobile app, a settings page beyond a theme toggle.

Finish with:
- npm install and npm run dev working from a clean clone.
- README.md with setup, the keyboard shortcuts, where the database lives, and a short honest list of what this clone does not do compared to the real product.
